newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba holds rates, odds grow on late 97 rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba holds rates, odds grow on late 97 rise.

text.p: The Bundesbank held its key interest rates steady on Thursday, despite the weakness of the German economy, and analysts said its next rate move could be up, not down.

The German central bank may be forced to shift gears -- raising not lowering interest rates -- sooner than expected and perhaps even before the year-end, if a firm dollar helps stoke up German prices, economists said.

Despite record unemployment, prompting calls for the Bundesbank to aid economic recovery with more expansive monetary policies, other data, particularly the outlook for prices, has changed official views, they said.
"Rate cuts are definitely no longer on the agenda," said Joachim Fels, economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
The Bundesbank, as expected, left its discount rate at 2.50 percent, the Lombard rate at 4.50 percent and its main money market rate, the repo, at three percent.

Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm, asked on Tuesday whether another rate cut might be possible, appeared to dash lingering hopes for an easing, explaining that he saw no reasons to abandon the bank's steady-hand policy now.

Although Palm and other Bundesbank officials still praise Germany's low inflation rate, running below two percent, and say that the mark's recent weakening does not worry them, economists predict that this relaxed picture could soon darken.

Import prices jumped 2.6 percent in the year to January and the Bundesbank reported 2.2 percent annual growth in fourth-quarter 1996 gross domestic product, suggesting that a stronger growth scenario could be emerging, which might demand tighter monetary policy.
Eckhard Schulte, economist at IBJ in Frankfurt, said the combination of new factors prompted him to bring forward his forecast for an interest rate hike to occur early next year.

Morgan Stanley's Fels tipped an even speedier schedule, saying "there is still a window of opportunity for a rate hike in the fourth quarter 1997", stressing, however, that the Bundesbank would then act only if inflation accelerated past two percent.

The Bundesbank kicked off this cycle of easing its policy in September 1992 by knocking 50 basis points off a record 8.75 percent discount rate. It has chipped away at rates ever since, moving the discount rate down to its current historic low in April 1996.
One key factor for German interest rates may now be the stronger dollar and its knock-on effect on German import, wholesale and eventually consumer prices, economists said.

"The Bundesbank can still tolerate the dollar at 1.70 marks but if it gets past 1.75 marks, they will get nervous, feeling the impact immediately on import prices. Then they will no longer ignore the currency situation," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch in Frankfurt.

A possible U.S. interest rate hike would not, however, have an automatic or direct impact on German rates, economists said, although there could be indirect consequences if the dollar were to advance further on any rate increase by the Federal Reserve.
"There would only be an indirect impact on Germany through the exchange rate situation," Fels said.

While Bundesbank officials still say inflation poses no current problems, economists say the authorities would not be blind to future problems and might become even tougher in battling inflation as Europe prepares for monetary union.

With only two years before the Bundesbank is set to cede control of monetary policy, it is expected to try its best to leave the future European central bank with low inflation rates, ideal conditions for a stable common currency.

Consequently, a swing higher in German interest rates might be very abrupt -- possibly beginning with a 20 basis point rise in the repo, followed by another repo rate hike coupled with a 25 basis point rise in the discount rate, economists said.

It would be unlikely, however, that the bank would revert to its preferred system of letting the market help set rates through variable rate repos, as this could quickly throw the central bank's fine-tuning mechanisms off-track.
While several economists now bet on a speedier shift in policies, others stick by predictions that the Bundesbank will not raise rates again before the European Central Bank assumes control in 1999.
But Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs, argues that such a scenario would not be motivated by a sudden laxness in fighting inflation but rather by political pressures.

As the starting date for European monetary union approaches and Germany scrambles to fulfil entry conditions, the Bundesbank "will not be in a position to raise interest rates until every last person realises such a step would not be taken to endanger the timely start of monetary union," Mayer said.
